scenes.narration: You want Claude to reach your GitHub, your Slack, your database. That plumbing is weeks of work.

scenes.headline: Why a standard [had to exist]
scenes.caption: the multiplication
scenes.premise: Every app that wants a tool, times every tool that exists. Without a standard, somebody writes each square.
scenes.narration: It's worth seeing why anyone bothered inventing a protocol, because the answer is a multiplication. ^Say there are four apps that want tool access — your editor, a chat client, an I D E, a terminal agent. ^And four services worth reaching: GitHub, Slack, Postgres, the filesystem. ^Without a standard, that's sixteen separate integrations, because every app writes its own version of every connection, and none of that work is shareable. ^With a standard, it's four servers and four clients — eight pieces instead of sixteen, and the numbers diverge fast as either side grows. That's the entire economic argument for MCP, and it's why the shape caught on so quickly.

scenes.headline: Server, client, [and a wire]
scenes.caption: the two words
scenes.premise: Your app is the client. Somebody else's program is the server. Every arrow is one JSON-RPC message crossing between them.
scenes.narration: So concretely, here's the shape. Your app opens a connection to a server, |and the first thing your app asks is what can you do. ^The server answers with a list of tools, each carrying a name and a description. |Then when you want one of those tools run, your app calls it by name with arguments, ^and the server runs the function and hands back the result. That's the entire protocol at this level — a question, a list, a call, a result — which means everything else in this course hangs off those four messages. Everything else in this course is detail hanging off those four messages.

lines.detail: Ask the server what it can do.
Run one, by name, with arguments.

scenes.narration: A server is somebody else's integration, packaged. That's MCP. Full course on the channel.
